title: Sandhya: water for the rising sun
word: the Gayatri and the peace chants
hookLine: demons at sunrise, water in cupped hands, and whose light the Gayatri means
carry: at sandhya, water for the sun, light for the mind
tomorrow: excellent, adorable, worth choosing: which does varenyam say?

cards: Phones come out at sunrise on any beach, and not everyone agrees on what they're photographing. Some see the sun. Some see what the sun stands for.
Readers of the Gayatri have split the same way for a long time. Its second word is savitur, of Savitr. Is that the sun in the sky, or something the sun only hints at?
The honest answer: inside the tradition, both readings have their defenders. Here are both, at their best.

teach.b: First the grammar, briefly. The god's name is Savitr; savitur means of Savitr. The radiance is his.
In the Rig Veda's hymns, Savitr rouses the day and sets the world moving. Now a story about why the Gayatri meets the sun.
In the Vishnu Purana, demons called the Mandehas try to devour the sun every morning as it rises.
And every morning, brahmins at prayer cup water in their hands, say the Gayatri over it and throw it toward the sun, and the water strikes the demons like thunderbolts. The sun comes up.
That's one story behind sandhya, the prayer at the joining times of the day, dawn, noon and dusk, with an offering of water to the sun called arghya.
You can still see it: someone at a river or on a balcony, palms full of water, facing east.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: THE REAL SUN. VIEW TWO: A LIGHT WITHIN.
teach.b: So, view one: the Gayatri belongs to a real morning and a real sun, a body standing in the light. Its strength is the practice itself.

View two: some teachers, reading the Upanishads, hear Savitr's radiance as an inner light too, the light by which the mind sees anything at all. Its strength: the verse asks for thoughts to be stirred, not crops to grow.
Many families hold both: the water goes to the sun outside, and the prayer asks for the light inside. Savitur says whose the radiance is, and leaves the rest to the one praying.

how: In sandhya-vandana, many Hindus offer water (arghya) to the sun with the Gayatri at dawn, noon and dusk; the Vishnu Purana tells that this water drives off the Mandeha demons. Some teachers also explain Savitr's radiance as an inner light that wakes the mind. Both readings are taught.

games.q: what does “the gayatri and the peace chants” mean?
o: a festival where the sun is hidden for a whole day

s: savitur and Savitr are two different gods
savitur is Savitr's name with an ending: of Savitr.
at sandhya, many Hindus offer water to the sun with the Gayatri
the arghya, at the joining times of the day.
the tradition holds one fixed answer to what Savitr's radiance is
some hear the sun's own light; some teachers hear an inner light too. both are taught.

games.q: Sam says the Gayatri is 'basically a sun prayer, nothing deeper.' before Priya answers, what's the best case for Sam's side?
o: Savitr is the god who rouses the day, and at sandhya people throw water to the rising sun with the Gayatri.
the word savitur simply means sun, and has no other meaning.
the Gayatri never names any god, so only the sun is left.
games.why: Sam's best case stands on the practice: arghya to the sun at the joining times. the inner reading has its own best case: the verse asks for thoughts to be stirred. many families hold both.

practice: If you keep sandhya, this is a fine moment for it, as you were taught.
If not, turn your body toward the brightest direction near you, a window or a lamp, sit tall with your palms resting on your knees, and feel the light on your face for a few breaths.
Then, still facing it, notice the seeing itself, the part of you that knows there's light.

wordCard.voice: The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: savitur, of Savitr, the god whose light Hindus greet with water at the joining times of the day.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: Savitr, the god whose radiance the Gayatri holds in mind; savitur means of Savitr.
